title: Hard to find
hook: a free Saturday slides by on the couch; Shantideva says a day like it is hard to find
carry: a precious human life: rarer than the turtle's yoke
tomorrow: a good thought shows up. why is it gone so fast?

segments.voice: Yesterday the poem opened: the Bodhicaryavatara, Shantideva's guide to living for others. A poem for living. Now its first real argument, and it starts with a turtle.
screen: `A POEM FOR LIVING.` → `NOW: ITS FIRST ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: A Saturday with nothing on it. No shift, no practice, no family thing. It shows up maybe once a season, and here's how it usually goes: you wake late, you pick up the phone to check one thing, and the next time you look up the light has moved across the floor. Nothing went wrong. Nobody got hurt. The day just slid off the table. Shantideva noticed that same slide, about a whole life instead of a day, and he answered it with a picture from an older sermon.
screen: `A SATURDAY WITH NOTHING ON IT.` → `CHECK ONE THING.` → `THE DAY SLIDES OFF THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the picture, from the Pali suttas. The Buddha asks his monks to see the whole earth as one ocean. Somewhere on it floats a wooden yoke with a single hole, pushed east by one wind, west by another. Down in the deep lives a blind turtle that comes up once every hundred years. Would it ever put its neck through that hole? Only by chance, the monks say. So too, the Buddha says, it is by chance that one gets a human life. Shantideva takes that and turns it toward today. In the first chapter of his poem, he says this human life, with its leisure and its opportunity, is very hard to find, and it can do what a life is for. If no good comes of it now, he asks, when will a chance like this come round again? Leisure here doesn't mean a day off. It means the freedoms you might skip past: a mind clear enough to think, a little time that isn't pure survival, a teaching within reach. The verse isn't trying to scare anyone. It's closer to a friend grabbing your arm at a window: look at this. Hard to find, and you're standing in it.
screen: `ONE OCEAN, ONE YOKE, ONE BLIND TURTLE.` · `ONLY BY CHANCE.` · `LEISURE AND OPPORTUNITY.` · `NOT A THREAT: LOOK AT THIS.` · then, large: `HARD TO FIND.`

segments.voice: Name one freedom you have right now, out loud, in plain words: I can read. I have this hour. Someone taught me this. Say it once, slowly, then sit with it for the rest of the time, the way you'd look at something you almost walked past.
Hard to find. Shantideva's name for this life with room in it: leisure, opportunity, a teaching nearby. Rare as a blind turtle finding the yoke.
Your line: a precious human life, rarer than the turtle's yoke. The turtle found the hole once; you're already through it. Two days into the poem.

screen: `DAY 1457 COUNTS.` → `SHANTIDEVA'S GUIDE · 2 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: A GOOD THOUGHT SHOWS UP. WHY IS IT GONE SO FAST?`

howItsDone: Some Tibetan teachers open a course on the Bodhicaryavatara with this verse on the precious human life, and the blind turtle from the Pali suttas is told in more than one Buddhist school as a reminder of how rare the chance is.

myth: the precious human life teaching is meant to make you feel guilty
the verse reads more like a friend at a window: look at this. it points at a chance, not a failure.

fork.setup: a friend says, "life's short, so i just try to enjoy it." how does Shantideva's verse use that same fact?
options: the same way: a rare life is for enjoying while it lasts.
a life with leisure is a rare chance to do what a life is for, so use it for good now.
the opposite: life is long, so there's no hurry to practice.
fork.reveal: Shantideva agrees the chance is rare. that's exactly why he asks: if no good comes of it now, when will a chance like this come round again?

original.note: Sanskrit: hard to get, rare. Shantideva's verse calls this human life very hard to find.

trapdoor: what you thought: a precious human life is a nice saying about being grateful.
what it means: this life, with leisure and opportunity, is rare, and it can do what a life is for, so the time to use it is now.
what a scholar hears: Shantideva's first chapter takes up the old image of the blind turtle and the yoke from the Samyutta Nikaya and makes it his opening argument.
guess: this life with room to learn, rare and easy to waste
a teaching too difficult for most people to grasp
a hidden temple that only monks know how to reach

chat.says: ông keeps saying "this human life is hard to find." kinda grim?? what does he mean
options: Not grim. Like the blind turtle: a life with room to learn and do good is rare. He's grateful.
It's a warning that life is short, so he wants you to worry less and party more.
It means only monks have a precious life; everyone else just waits their turn.
chat.meaning: Shantideva calls a life with leisure and opportunity hard to find, rare as the blind turtle surfacing through the yoke. It's a chance to use for good, not a reason to fear.

tie.story: The Buddha told of a blind turtle rising once a century into the one hole of a floating yoke; a human life, he said, is that rare.
tie.friend: Mai can hear ông's line as gratitude: this life is a rare chance to learn and do good.
tie.you: What's one freedom you have right now?

Shantideva.meaning: the Buddhist monk and poet who wrote the Bodhicaryavatara

Bodhicaryavatara.meaning: Shantideva's poem: a guide to the bodhisattva's way of life

suttas.meaning: the Buddha's discourses in the Pali canon

yoke.meaning: a wooden frame for an ox's neck; here, floating with one hole

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 1.4 (this human life with leisure and opportunity is very hard to find)
Samyutta Nikaya 56.48 (Chiggala Sutta: the blind turtle and the yoke)

notes: No public-domain English translation of the Bodhicaryavatara is on our list (Barnett's 1909 'The Path of Light' is abridged and not on the validator list), so every Shantideva verse in this block is paraphrased with quoted: null. Verse numbers follow the Sanskrit edition; Tibetan numbering differs in places. Confirm references.

'Leisure and opportunity' renders kshana-sampad (1.4); later Tibetan teachers count specific freedoms and endowments, which the lesson deliberately doesn't number. Confirm the gloss of leisure as room to think and meet a teaching.

The blind turtle: SN 56.48 says the turtle surfaces once every hundred years and that a human birth comes 'by chance'; the lesson keeps that number because the cited sutta states it. Confirm against the Pali.
Original game: durlabha (दुर्लभ, hard to get); the verse has sudurlabha, 'very hard to find'. Confirm.
